questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?
questions.answer: **B.** Kepler's first law: planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. The Sun is not at the geometric centre, planets move more slowly further out, and $T^2\propto r^3$, so doubling $r$ multiplies $T$ by $2^{3/2}\approx 2.8$.
options: The Sun is in the exact geometric centre of our solar system.
The orbits of planets around the Sun are in the shape of an ellipse.
Planets move faster in their orbits the further away they are from the Sun.
A planet that is twice as far away from the Sun as the Earth will take twice as long as the Earth to complete its orbit.

questions.question: An object is in a planet's gravitational field. When does the gravitational potential energy of the object approach zero?
questions.answer: **D.** $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ approaches zero only as $r\to\infty$.
options: When its acceleration is $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$
When it is on the surface of a planet
When it is in outer space
When it approaches an infinite distance from the planet

questions.question:
A bullet is fired into the air and follows the flight path shown.

If all effects due to air friction are negligible while the bullet is in flight, which of the following statements is true?
questions.answer: **A.** With no air resistance the only force is gravity, so the acceleration is a constant $g$ downwards and the total mechanical energy ($K+U$) is conserved.
options: The energy and acceleration of the bullet remain constant.
The energy of the bullet varies while the acceleration remains constant.
The energy of the bullet remains constant while the acceleration varies.
Both the energy and acceleration of the bullet vary while in flight.

questions.question:
An experiment was repeated several times in an attempt to measure Earth's gravitational acceleration at the surface of the Earth. The results are shown below.

| Trial number | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Result (m s$^{-2}$) | 8.80 | 8.82 | 8.79 | 8.81 | 8.78 |

It would be true to say that this experiment was:
questions.answer: **C.** The results are very close to one another (reliable) but all are well below the accepted value of $9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ (not accurate), suggesting a systematic error.
options: accurate and reliable.
accurate but not reliable.
not accurate but reliable.
not accurate and not reliable.

questions.question:
An object is travelling around a circular track at a constant speed of $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. It moves anticlockwise and is currently at the rightmost point of the circle (directly to the right of the centre).

Which describes the directions of the velocity $v$ and acceleration $a$ of the object at this position?
questions.answer: **A.** The velocity is tangential (up the page for anticlockwise motion at the right-hand point) and the centripetal acceleration points towards the centre (to the left).
options: $v$ up the page, $a$ to the left
$v$ up the page, $a$ to the right
$v$ up the page, $a=0$
$v$ up the page, $a$ up the page

questions.question:
Two charges, $a$ and $b$, of equal magnitude enter the electric field between parallel plates at the same speed. Their subsequent motions are shown.

Qualitatively, the mass of $a$:
questions.answer:
**A.** Both charges cross a similar vertical distance, but $a$ does so while travelling a much shorter horizontal distance, so it takes less time at the same initial speed and has the larger acceleration. Since $a=\dfrac{qE}{m}$ with equal $q$ and $E$, particle $a$ has the smaller mass.

*Note: the school's key gives B, but the more sharply deflected particle $a$ must be the lighter one.*
options: is less than the mass of $b$.
is greater than the mass of $b$.
is equal to the mass of $b$.
cannot be decided without further data.

questions.question: Calculate the flux in a magnetic field when its flux density is $5000\ \mu\text{T}$ and its cross-sectional area is $300\ \text{mm}^2$.
A transformer is designed to convert 240 V AC mains to 12 V, and has 4000 turns on its primary coil. The number of turns on its secondary coil should be:

The figure shows two metal rings arranged concentrically. The current in the outer ring is anticlockwise. Using Lenz's law, find the direction of the induced current in the inner ring when the current in the outer ring is decreased.
questions.answer: **B.** The anticlockwise current produces flux out of the page inside the rings. As it decreases, the induced current opposes the loss of flux by producing flux out of the page, so it is anticlockwise.
options: Clockwise
Anticlockwise
Into the page
Out of the page

questions.question:
A source of unpolarised light is viewed through two crossed polarising filters X and Y.

Which correctly describes the light emerging from the two filters?
questions.answer: **D.** X transmits light oscillating in one plane only. Y's axis is at $90^\circ$ to X, so $I=I_{max}\cos^2 90^\circ=0$.
options: From X: oscillates in every direction. From Y: oscillates in one direction.
From X: oscillates in every direction. From Y: no light.
From X: oscillates in one direction. From Y: oscillates in one direction.
From X: oscillates in one direction. From Y: no light.

questions.question: What is the minimum distance between the walls of a resonant cavity that will sustain a standing EM wave with a frequency of $2.31\times10^{9}$ Hz?
questions.answer: **A.** $\lambda=\dfrac{c}{f}=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{2.31\times10^9}=0.130$ m. The shortest standing wave has nodes at both walls and length $\lambda/2=0.065$ m.

questions.question:
A beam of light is passed through an interferometer as shown.

If there is a difference in path length between paths 1 and 2 of half a wavelength, what will the interference pattern show on the screen?
questions.answer: **B.** A path difference of $\lambda/2$ means the recombining beams arrive out of phase at the centre and interfere destructively, giving a central dark spot (with fringes around it).
options: A bright spot in the centre
A dark spot in the centre
Total brightness on the whole screen
Total darkness on the whole screen

questions.question: The Big Bang theory is best described as:
questions.answer: **C.** It is a scientific theory, supported by evidence such as galactic redshift and the cosmic microwave background, that explains the origin and early evolution of the Universe.
options: the way in which we know that the Universe began.
a theory that explains the reason for the accelerating expansion of the Universe.
a theory based on observations and measurements that explains how the Universe began.
a theory that explains how the elements were formed.

questions.question: The Hubble constant, $H_0$, relates which concepts?
questions.answer: **A.** Hubble's law $v=H_0 d$ relates the recession speed of a galaxy to its distance.
options: speed of expansion of the Universe and the distance from Earth
speed of the expanding Universe and the age of the Universe
volume of the Universe and the age of the Universe
acceleration of the expanding Universe and the distance from Earth

questions.question: Atom X undergoes alpha decay to form atom Y. How will the nucleus of Y be different from that of X?
questions.answer: **D.** An alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), which the parent nucleus loses.
options: Y will have 2 more protons than X.
Y will have 2 fewer protons but the same number of neutrons as X.
Y will have 2 more protons and 2 more neutrons than X.
Y will have 2 fewer protons and 2 fewer neutrons than X.

questions.question: According to the spectra shown, which combination of elements does the unknown star most likely contain?
questions.answer: **B.** Every line of iron and every line of calcium appears in the star's absorption spectrum, and together they account for all of its lines. Sodium's close pair of lines is absent.
options: calcium and sodium
calcium and iron
iron and magnesium
sodium, iron and magnesium

questions.question: As an object becomes hotter, its colour changes from red, to orange, to yellow and then white, not green. This is because:
questions.answer: **D.** Black-body radiation is a broad continuous spectrum. When the peak lies near green, strong red and blue light are also emitted and the mixture is perceived as white.
options: green light is much harder for the human eye to detect.
green is not a part of the colour spectrum.
without blue, green cannot be produced.
by this stage a mixture of all the colours in the visible spectrum causes our brains to interpret the colour as white rather than green.

questions.question:
The graph shows the relationship between the square of the period and the cube of the distance from the centre of Jupiter for four of its moons.

Calculate the gradient of the graph.
questions.answer:
Using two well-separated points on the line, $(0,0)$ and $(450\times10^{25}\ \text{m}^3,\ 140\times10^{10}\ \text{s}^2)$:
$$m=\frac{140\times10^{10}-0}{450\times10^{25}-0}\approx 3.1\times10^{-16}\ \text{s}^2\,\text{m}^{-3}$$

questions.question:
The graph shows the relationship between the square of the period and the cube of the distance from the centre of Jupiter for four of its moons.

Use the gradient of the graph to calculate the mass of Jupiter.
questions.answer:
Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r^3}{T^2}=\dfrac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, so $T^2=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$ and the gradient is $m=\dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}$.

Reading the line, $m\approx3.1\times10^{-16}\ \text{s}^2\,\text{m}^{-3}$, so
$$M=\frac{4\pi^2}{Gm}=\frac{4\pi^2}{(6.67\times10^{-11})(3.1\times10^{-16})}\approx1.9\times10^{27}\ \text{kg}$$

questions.question:
In a hammer throw, a steel ball (the hammer) of mass 7.62 kg attached to a metal chain 1.20 m long is whirled at high speed in a circle and then released. The hammer was 1.80 m above ground level at the moment of release and the launch angle was $43^\circ$. By the time it had fallen back to 1.80 m above ground level it had travelled a horizontal distance of 86.0 m (total throw 88.74 m).

The range of a projectile that lands at its launch height is $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$. Use this to determine the speed of the hammer at the moment of release.
questions.answer: $$u=\sqrt{\frac{Rg}{\sin2\theta}}=\sqrt{\frac{86.0\times9.8}{\sin86^\circ}}\approx29\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
In a hammer throw, a steel ball (the hammer) of mass 7.62 kg attached to a metal chain 1.20 m long is whirled at high speed in a circle and then released. The hammer was 1.80 m above ground level at the moment of release and the launch angle was $43^\circ$. By the time it had fallen back to 1.80 m above ground level it had travelled a horizontal distance of 86.0 m (total throw 88.74 m).

The range of a projectile that lands at its launch height is $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$. Assuming that, at the moment of release, the hammer was rotating in a circle of radius 2.23 m, find its centripetal acceleration just before release.
questions.answer:
From the range formula, $u=\sqrt{\dfrac{86.0\times9.8}{\sin86^\circ}}=29.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
$$a_c=\frac{v^2}{r}=\frac{29.07^2}{2.23}\approx3.8\times10^2\ \text{m s}^{-2}\text{ towards the centre of the circle}$$

questions.question:
In a hammer throw, a steel ball (the hammer) of mass 7.62 kg attached to a metal chain 1.20 m long is whirled at high speed in a circle and then released. The hammer was 1.80 m above ground level at the moment of release and the launch angle was $43^\circ$. By the time it had fallen back to 1.80 m above ground level it had travelled a horizontal distance of 86.0 m (total throw 88.74 m).

The release speed is $29.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the hammer was rotating in a circle of radius 2.23 m. Calculate the force the athlete was applying to the handle of the chain just before releasing the hammer (ignore the weight of the hammer and chain).
questions.answer: $$F=\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{7.62\times29.07^2}{2.23}\approx2.9\times10^3\ \text{N}$$

questions.question:
In a hammer throw, a steel ball (the hammer) of mass 7.62 kg attached to a metal chain 1.20 m long is whirled at high speed in a circle and then released. The hammer was 1.80 m above ground level at the moment of release and the launch angle was $43^\circ$. By the time it had fallen back to 1.80 m above ground level it had travelled a horizontal distance of 86.0 m (total throw 88.74 m).

The release speed is $29.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Determine the kinetic energy of the hammer at the moment of release.
questions.answer: $$K=\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12(7.62)(29.07)^2\approx3.2\times10^3\ \text{J}$$

questions.question:
In a hammer throw, a steel ball (the hammer) of mass 7.62 kg attached to a metal chain 1.20 m long is whirled at high speed in a circle and then released. The hammer was 1.80 m above ground level at the moment of release and the launch angle was $43^\circ$. By the time it had fallen back to 1.80 m above ground level it had travelled a horizontal distance of 86.0 m (total throw 88.74 m).

The release speed is $29.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the radius of rotation is 2.23 m. Calculate the rate (in revolutions per minute) at which the athlete was spinning at the moment of release.
questions.answer:
Period of one revolution:
$$T=\frac{2\pi r}{v}=\frac{2\pi(2.23)}{29.07}=0.482\ \text{s}$$
$$\text{rate}=\frac{60}{T}\approx1.2\times10^2\ \text{revolutions per minute (about 125 rpm)}$$

questions.question:
A ball is launched with two different trajectories as shown: Trajectory 1 from ground level, and Trajectory 2 from the top of a platform. Neglect air resistance.

Describe the directions and relative magnitudes of the velocity and the acceleration of the ball at each of the points A, B and C on both trajectories.
questions.answer:
**Acceleration:** on both trajectories, at A, B and C, the acceleration is the same: $g$ vertically downwards.

**Velocity:** at every point it is tangent to the path in the direction of motion. The horizontal component is constant, and the speed is greater the lower the ball is.

- Trajectory 1: at A, up and to the right and the largest (lowest point); at B (just before the top), slightly up and to the right and the smallest; at C, down and to the right, intermediate. So $v_A>v_C>v_B$.
- Trajectory 2: at A (the top), horizontal and the smallest; at B, a little below horizontal and larger; at C, steeply downward and the largest. So $v_C>v_B>v_A$.

questions.question:
A ball is launched from ground level and lands at ground level (neglect air resistance), as shown.

Sketch graphs of the horizontal speed $v_x$ and the vertical speed $v_y$ of the ball against time throughout the flight.
questions.answer: $v_x$ is constant (no horizontal force). The vertical **speed** decreases uniformly to zero at the highest point, then increases uniformly at the same rate (slope magnitude $g$) back to its initial value.

questions.question:
A satellite is in a low-altitude polar orbit 850 km above the surface of the Earth. (Earth: $M=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.371\times10^{6}$ m.)

Find its period.

A satellite is in a low-altitude polar orbit 850 km above the surface of the Earth. (Earth: $M=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.371\times10^{6}$ m.)

Calculate how many times the satellite orbits the Earth in one day.
questions.answer:
The period is $T=2\pi\sqrt{r^3/GM}\approx6.10\times10^3$ s with $r=7.22\times10^6$ m.
$$n=\frac{86\,400}{6095}\approx14.2\ \text{orbits per day}$$

*Note: the school gets 14.1 by rounding the period to 1.7 h first.*

questions.question:
A satellite is in a low-altitude polar orbit 850 km above the surface of the Earth. (Earth: $M=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.371\times10^{6}$ m.)

Determine the speed of the satellite in its orbit.
questions.answer: $$v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{4.00\times10^{14}}{7.22\times10^6}}\approx7.44\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
A satellite is in a low-altitude polar orbit 850 km above the surface of the Earth. (Earth: $M=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.371\times10^{6}$ m.)

If the mass of the satellite is $m$ kg, determine the (total mechanical) energy of the satellite in its orbit.
questions.answer:
$$E=K+U=\frac{GMm}{2r}-\frac{GMm}{r}=-\frac{GMm}{2r}=-\frac{(4.00\times10^{14})m}{2(7.22\times10^6)}\approx-2.77\times10^7\,m\ \text{J}$$
(taking $U=0$ at infinity).

*Note: the school's answer, $+2.77\times10^7m$ J, is only the kinetic energy. The total energy of a bound orbit is negative.*

questions.question:
A satellite is in a low-altitude polar orbit 850 km above the surface of the Earth. (Earth: $M=6.0\times10^{24}$ kg, radius $6.371\times10^{6}$ m.)

Over 5 years, aerodynamic drag from the traces of atmosphere at this altitude removes energy from the satellite (the paper describes this as reducing its kinetic energy by 10%). Describe qualitatively the effect this has on the altitude of the satellite, and on the number of revolutions per day about the Earth.
questions.answer:
Drag initially slows the satellite, so gravity is more than the centripetal force needed at that radius and the satellite moves inwards: its **altitude decreases** and its total energy becomes more negative.

At the smaller radius the orbital period is shorter ($T^2\propto r^3$), so the satellite completes **more revolutions per day**.

*Note: once it has settled into the lower orbit the satellite is actually moving faster, not slower ($v=\sqrt{GM/r}$): the potential energy lost exceeds the work done against drag. So the premise that drag leaves it with 10% less kinetic energy is not physically right.*

questions.question:
The diagram shows a generator connected through a switch to a light globe.

Identify the type of generator, giving a thorough explanation for your answer.
questions.answer: It is an **AC generator**. Each end of the coil is joined to its own **slip ring**, so each side of the coil stays connected to the same brush throughout the rotation. As the coil turns, the rate of change of flux through it reverses sign every half revolution, so the emf and current supplied to the globe reverse direction every half cycle. (A DC generator would use a split-ring commutator.)

questions.question:
The diagram shows a generator connected through a switch to a light globe.

Initially the plane of the coil is vertical, as shown, and the switch is closed. The generator is rotated through one revolution in the first second and then two revolutions in the next second. Sketch a graph of current against time for the two seconds.
questions.answer:
At $t=0$ the coil is perpendicular to the field (maximum flux, zero rate of change), so the current starts at zero.

- 0–1 s: one sinusoidal cycle of period 1 s and amplitude $I_0$.
- 1–2 s: two cycles of period 0.5 s. Doubling the rotation rate doubles the rate of change of flux, so the amplitude is $2I_0$.

(The direction taken as positive is arbitrary.)

questions.question:
The diagram shows a generator connected through a switch to a light globe.

If the generator is rotated at a steady pace, state one modification you would need to make to the generator design to ensure a steady emf is generated, and explain why.
questions.answer:
Replace the slip rings with a **split-ring commutator and use many coils set at different angles** around the axis (each connected to its own pair of commutator segments).

The commutator keeps the output in one direction, and with many coils the brushes always connect to a coil that is near the position of maximum rate of change of flux, so the emf stays nearly constant instead of rising and falling.

*Note: the school also suggests radial magnets. A radial field gives an emf of nearly constant size, but with slip rings it still reverses every half turn, so it is not steady on its own.*

questions.question:
A Physics class builds a model of a transmission system, shown below, to investigate power loss in transmission lines. It has a variable voltage AC supply, two transmission lines each of resistance 4.0 Ω in series, a step-down transformer with a turns ratio of 4:1, a 4.0 V light globe and meters. The globe is operating at its rated voltage and the current in the transmission lines is 3.0 A. Assume the transformer is ideal.

Calculate the power dissipated in the light globe.
questions.answer:
The transformer steps the voltage down by 4 and so the current up by 4: $I_s=4\times3.0=12$ A.
$$P=VI=4.0\times12=48\ \text{W}$$

questions.question:
A Physics class builds a model of a transmission system, shown below, to investigate power loss in transmission lines. It has a variable voltage AC supply, two transmission lines each of resistance 4.0 Ω in series, a step-down transformer with a turns ratio of 4:1, a 4.0 V light globe and meters. The globe is operating at its rated voltage and the current in the transmission lines is 3.0 A. Assume the transformer is ideal.

Calculate the total power loss in the transmission lines.
questions.answer:
Total line resistance $=2\times4.0=8.0\ \Omega$.
$$P_{loss}=I^2R=3.0^2\times8.0=72\ \text{W}$$

questions.question:
A Physics class builds a model of a transmission system, shown below, to investigate power loss in transmission lines. It has a variable voltage AC supply, two transmission lines each of resistance 4.0 Ω in series, a step-down transformer with a turns ratio of 4:1, a 4.0 V light globe and meters. The globe is operating at its rated voltage and the current in the transmission lines is 3.0 A. Assume the transformer is ideal.

Calculate the voltage output of the power supply.
questions.answer:
Primary voltage of the transformer: $V_p=4\times4.0=16$ V.

Voltage drop along the lines: $V=IR=3.0\times8.0=24$ V.

Supply voltage: $16+24=40$ V.

questions.question: The loop shown has a diameter of 16.0 cm and 42 windings. It is pushed completely into an 8.70 T magnetic field (the dots show the field directed out of the page) in 0.0140 s. What is the average emf, and in what direction does the current flow?
questions.answer:
$$\Delta\Phi=BA=8.70\times\pi(0.080)^2=0.175\ \text{Wb}$$
$$\varepsilon=N\frac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}=\frac{42\times0.175}{0.0140}\approx525\ \text{V}$$

Flux out of the page through the loop is increasing, so by Lenz's law the induced current produces a field into the page: the current flows **clockwise** (viewed from the front).

*Note: the school says anticlockwise. That would be correct for a field into the page (crosses), not the dots shown.*

questions.question:
The diagram represents two circuits with 4.0 A of current flowing through each. Section RQ is 0.01 m vertically above section LM, and RQ and LM are each 0.03 m long. The coil RTUQ is pivoted at S and P.

Calculate the magnetic force acting between LM and RQ.
questions.answer:
$$F=\frac{\mu_0 I_1I_2\,l}{2\pi r}=\frac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(4.0)(4.0)(0.03)}{2\pi(0.01)}=9.6\times10^{-6}\ \text{N}$$
The currents in RQ and LM are in the same direction, so the force is **attractive** (RQ is pulled down towards LM).

*Note: the school's answer, $96\times10^{7}$ N, uses $2\times10^{7}$ instead of $2\times10^{-7}$.*

questions.question:
The diagram represents two circuits with 4.0 A of current flowing through each. Section RQ is 0.01 m vertically above section LM, and RQ and LM are each 0.03 m long. The coil RTUQ is pivoted at S and P.

A mass $m$ is placed on the other end of the coil at the same distance from the pivot as RQ. Calculate the size of the mass which will exactly balance the magnetic force between LM and RQ.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force on RQ is $F=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2l}{2\pi r}=9.6\times10^{-6}$ N. With equal distances from the pivot, torques balance when $mg=F$:
$$m=\frac{9.6\times10^{-6}}{9.8}\approx9.8\times10^{-7}\ \text{kg}\ (0.98\ \text{mg})$$

*Note: the school's $9.6\times10^{7}$ kg follows from its sign error in the power of ten.*

questions.question:
A square coil of wire of 250 turns with sides 4 cm × 4 cm is attached to a split-ring commutator and a power source providing 2 A. A student placed permanent magnets at A and B and the motor started spinning. Using a torque meter on the axle, the student measured the torque at various angles θ and plotted torque (N m) against cos θ as shown.

Use the graph and the information given to calculate the strength of the magnetic field provided by the magnets. Show all working.
questions.answer:
$\tau=nBIA\cos\theta$, so a graph of $\tau$ against $\cos\theta$ is a straight line with gradient $nBIA$.

From the line of best fit, gradient $\approx56\ \text{N m}$.
$$B=\frac{\text{gradient}}{nIA}=\frac{56}{250\times2\times(0.04)^2}\approx70\ \text{T}$$

*Note: this follows from the plotted data, although a field of about 70 T is far larger than any permanent magnet could provide.*

questions.question:
A student wants to use the stationary waves formed in a microwave oven (shown below) to measure the frequency of the microwaves emitted by the transmitter.

Explain how stationary waves are formed in the microwave oven.
questions.answer: Microwaves from the transmitter are reflected by the metal oven walls. The reflected waves superpose (interfere) with the incident waves of the same frequency travelling in the opposite direction. This produces a stationary wave, with fixed nodes where the interference is always destructive and fixed antinodes where the amplitude is maximum.

questions.question:
A student wants to use the stationary waves formed in a microwave oven (shown below) to measure the frequency of the microwaves emitted by the transmitter.

The student removes the turntable, places a bar of chocolate on the floor of the oven and switches the oven on for about a minute. Three small patches of melted chocolate are observed, as shown in the second diagram.

The two outer patches are 11.8 cm apart (measured on the original figure). Use this to calculate the frequency of the microwaves.
questions.answer:
Adjacent patches are at adjacent antinodes, which are $\lambda/2$ apart. The outer patches span two such intervals, so $\lambda=0.118$ m.
$$f=\frac{c}{\lambda}=\frac{3.00\times10^8}{0.118}\approx2.5\times10^9\ \text{Hz}$$

questions.question:
A student wants to use the stationary waves formed in a microwave oven (shown below) to measure the frequency of the microwaves emitted by the transmitter.

The student removes the turntable, places a bar of chocolate on the floor of the oven and switches the oven on for about a minute. Three small patches of melted chocolate are observed, as shown in the second diagram.

Explain why the chocolate melts at these points only.
questions.answer: These points are antinodes of the stationary wave, where the amplitude and therefore the energy delivered to the chocolate are maximum. At and near the nodes there is little or no energy transferred.

questions.question:
A student wants to use the stationary waves formed in a microwave oven (shown below) to measure the frequency of the microwaves emitted by the transmitter.

Explain why a microwave oven has a rotating turntable for cooking food.
questions.answer: The antinodes are fixed in place, so rotating the food moves all parts of it through regions of high intensity. This heats it more evenly and avoids hot and cold spots.

questions.question:
A student obtains the following diffraction pattern on a wall by shining a red laser beam through a single narrow slit. The corresponding graph of intensity against position is also shown.

Explain how this diffraction pattern is created.
questions.answer:
Light behaves as a wave, so on passing through the narrow slit it spreads out (diffracts). By Huygens' principle, each point across the slit acts as a source of secondary wavelets, all initially in phase.

The wavelets from different parts of the slit travel different distances to a given point on the wall, so they arrive with different phase relationships and superpose.

Where they largely arrive in phase they interfere constructively and give a bright region; where they cancel in pairs (path difference between the two edges equal to a whole number of wavelengths) they interfere destructively and give a dark minimum. At the centre all path lengths are nearly equal, giving a broad, very bright central maximum, with progressively fainter maxima on either side.

questions.question:
A narrow beam of monochromatic light of wavelength 590 nm is directed normally at a diffraction grating with grating spacing $1.67\times10^{-6}$ m.

Calculate the angle of diffraction of the second-order diffracted beam.
questions.answer: $$\sin\theta=\frac{m\lambda}{d}=\frac{2\times590\times10^{-9}}{1.67\times10^{-6}}=0.707\ \Rightarrow\ \theta\approx45^\circ$$

questions.question:
A narrow beam of monochromatic light of wavelength 590 nm is directed normally at a diffraction grating with grating spacing $1.67\times10^{-6}$ m.

Show that no order higher than the second can be observed at this wavelength.
questions.answer: For the third order, $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3\times590\times10^{-9}}{1.67\times10^{-6}}=1.06>1$, which is impossible. Higher orders give even larger values, so the second order is the highest observable.

questions.question:
The graph shows how the maximum kinetic energy $T$ of photoelectrons emitted from the surface of sodium metal varies with the frequency $f$ of the incident electromagnetic radiation.

Use the graph to find a value for the Planck constant and the work function of sodium.
questions.answer:
$T=hf-\phi$, so the gradient is $h$ and the horizontal intercept is the threshold frequency $f_0$.

The line meets the axis at $f_0\approx5.5\times10^{14}$ Hz and passes near $(13.0\times10^{14},\,4.9\times10^{-19})$.
$$h=\frac{4.9\times10^{-19}-0}{(13.0-5.5)\times10^{14}}\approx6.6\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}$$
$$\phi=hf_0=(6.6\times10^{-34})(5.5\times10^{14})\approx3.6\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

*Note: the school quotes a work function of $-3.8\times10^{-19}$ J. The work function is positive ($-\phi$ is the vertical intercept), and the graph gives about $3.6\times10^{-19}$ J.*

questions.question:
The graph shows how the maximum kinetic energy $T$ of photoelectrons emitted from the surface of sodium metal varies with the frequency $f$ of the incident electromagnetic radiation.

Calculate the stopping voltage when the frequency of the incident radiation is $9.0\times10^{14}$ Hz.
questions.answer:
From the graph (or $T=h(f-f_0)$): $T\approx(6.6\times10^{-34})(9.0-5.5)\times10^{14}\approx2.3\times10^{-19}$ J.
$$eV_s=T\ \Rightarrow\ V_s=\frac{2.3\times10^{-19}}{1.60\times10^{-19}}\approx1.4\ \text{V}$$

*Note: the school's worked value of 1.35 V comes from using $\phi=3.8\times10^{-19}$ J.*

questions.question: Define polarisation.
questions.answer: Polarisation is the restriction of the oscillations of a transverse wave (for light, the electric field) to a single plane containing the direction of travel.

questions.question: A polariser and an analyser are rotated relative to each other. Find the ratio of the light intensity leaving the analyser to that incident on it when the angle between the sheets is $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$.
questions.answer:
Malus' law: $\dfrac{I}{I_{max}}=\cos^2\theta$.

- $30^\circ$: $0.75$
- $45^\circ$: $0.50$
- $60^\circ$: $0.25$

so the intensities are in the ratio $3:2:1$.

questions.question: Evaluate the importance of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram in our understanding of the evolution and life of stars.
questions.answer:
The Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram plots the luminosity (or absolute magnitude) of stars against their surface temperature (or spectral class), with temperature increasing to the left. Stars do not fall at random on it but form groups: the main sequence, red giants, supergiants and white dwarfs.

**Life on the main sequence.** About 90% of observed stars lie on the main sequence, which indicates that stars spend most of their lives there, fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores in a stable balance between gravity and outward pressure. Position along the sequence depends on mass: massive stars are hot and luminous and fuse mainly by the CNO cycle; low-mass stars are cool and dim and fuse by the proton–proton chain. Their luminosity shows that massive stars use their fuel far faster and live much shorter lives.

**Evolution.** A single star's evolution is too slow to watch, but the diagram captures many stars at different stages. Combined with models of stellar interiors, it lets astronomers trace tracks: a protostar contracts onto the main sequence; when core hydrogen runs out the star moves to the giant or supergiant region; Sun-like stars then shed their outer layers and end as white dwarfs, while very massive stars end as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes.

**Clusters.** Stars in a cluster formed at about the same time at about the same distance. The point where the cluster's main sequence turns off towards the giants shows which masses have already exhausted their hydrogen, and so gives the cluster's age. This is strong evidence that stars of different mass evolve at different rates.

**Limitations.** The diagram is a snapshot: on its own it does not show the direction or speed of evolution, which come from nuclear physics and computer modelling. Neutron stars and black holes are not shown on a standard diagram.

**Judgement.** The H–R diagram is of fundamental importance: it organises observations into patterns that theories of stellar evolution must explain and against which they are tested. It is not sufficient by itself, but without it our understanding of the life cycle of stars would be far weaker.

questions.question:
The H–R diagram for a cluster is shown below. Stars X and Z are both part of the same cluster but have different main sequence nuclear reactions and different evolutionary pathways.

Identify the fusion reactions in star X and star Z, giving reasons for your answer.
questions.answer:
**Star X:** mainly the **CNO cycle**. It is high on the main sequence (hot, luminous, more massive than the Sun), so its core is hot enough (above about $1.8\times10^7$ K) for the CNO cycle to dominate.

**Star Z:** mainly the **proton–proton chain**. It is lower on the main sequence (cooler, dimmer, less massive than the Sun), with a core temperature at which the proton–proton chain dominates.

questions.question:
The H–R diagram for a cluster is shown below. Stars X and Z are both part of the same cluster but have different main sequence nuclear reactions and different evolutionary pathways.

Predict TWO possible evolutionary pathways for star X.
questions.answer:
1. As a single star of a few solar masses: main sequence → red giant → ejects a planetary nebula → white dwarf.
2. If it is massive enough (more than about 8 solar masses, for example after gaining mass from a companion): supergiant → supernova → neutron star, or black hole for the most massive cores.

*Note: the school gives only the supernova route (ending as a neutron star or black hole). X's plotted luminosity, a few hundred times the Sun's, suggests a mass of only about 4–5 solar masses, for which a white dwarf is the expected end.*

questions.question: Find the missing particle or nucleus in this decay: ${}^{83}_{39}\text{Y}\rightarrow\ ?\ +\ \alpha$
questions.answer: Conserving mass number and charge: $A=83-4=79$, $Z=39-2=37$, so the nucleus is ${}^{79}_{37}\text{Rb}$.

questions.question: Find the missing particle or nucleus in this decay: $?\ \rightarrow\ {}^{49}_{22}\text{Ti}\ +\ \beta^-$
questions.answer: $A=49$ and $Z=22+(-1)=21$, so the parent is ${}^{49}_{21}\text{Sc}$ (an antineutrino is also emitted).

questions.question: Imagine it is possible for ${}^{14}_{7}\text{N}$ to undergo both $\beta^-$ and $\beta^+$ decay. Write the complete decay equation for each (including the neutrino or antineutrino).

What is the kinetic energy, in MeV, of the alpha particle ($m=4.002603$ u) that ${}^{208}\text{Po}$ ($m=207.981222$ u) gives off in becoming ${}^{204}\text{Pb}$ ($m=203.973020$ u)? (To convert u to MeV multiply by 931.5.)
questions.answer:
$$\Delta m=207.981222-(203.973020+4.002603)=0.005599\ \text{u}$$
$$E=0.005599\times931.5\approx5.22\ \text{MeV}$$
This assumes the alpha particle takes all the released energy, which is the intended answer.

*Note: strictly, momentum conservation gives the recoiling lead nucleus a share, so the alpha particle has $\tfrac{204}{208}\times5.22\approx5.12$ MeV.*

questions.question:
The spectrum of star X is observed at different times, with the results shown below the laboratory helium reference spectrum (the top row).

What can we learn from these images about star X, other than its chemical composition? Justify your answer.
questions.answer:
- **Its velocity along the line of sight changes periodically.** Compared with the reference, all the lines are shifted one way, then not at all, then the other way, then not at all. These are Doppler blue shifts and red shifts, so the star alternately approaches and recedes.
- **It is most likely orbiting a companion (a spectroscopic binary).** A regular alternation of this kind is what orbital motion produces; the unshifted observations occur when the star is moving across our line of sight.
- **It has no obvious overall motion towards or away from us**, since the shifts are about equal either side of the reference positions and average to zero.
- **It is not rotating very rapidly (as seen from Earth)**, since the lines stay narrow; rapid rotation would broaden them.

*Note: the school says the shifts show the star is rotating (and that helium lines show it is a red giant). Rotation of a star broadens its lines instead of shifting them all together, and chemical composition was excluded by the question.*
